Triggers.value: Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Making eye contact with other people
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it
I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself

Threat.value: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

vignette: Samantha, a 30-year-old married woman and bank teller, has been struggling to cope with the aftermath of torture she endured nearly two years ago. Her trauma manifests in several debilitating ways that have significantly impacted her daily life and relationships. On the day Samantha was tortured, she was forced into a small, silent room where she felt intensely watched by her captors. They expressed their anger at her through harsh words and physical violence. The silence before each new act was particularly terrifying; it made her feel as though something worse was just about to happen. These elements have become potent triggers that keep her in a constant state of vigilance. Samantha has found herself avoiding eye contact with others, especially those who might express anger, even calmly. She feels jumpy and easily startled by sudden movements or sounds, which reminds her of the torture she endured. The unusual silence in her surroundings often brings back the memory of that terrifying room where every moment felt like it could end in more pain. The memories of that day are vivid and overwhelming for Samantha. When they return to her mind, she experiences a full sensory reliving of those moments, which is so intense that she has to stop whatever she’s doing to cope with the emotional flood. This memory often comes back without warning, triggered by something in her surroundings, like the sound of someone raising their voice or feeling watched at work. Her overanalysing of the event and compulsive spending are coping mechanisms that have developed as a response to these overwhelming memories and threats she perceives around her. She spends money impulsively to distract herself from her distress, buying things she doesn’t need but finds comfort in the temporary relief it provides. When she recalls the traumatic event, she goes over every detail, trying to make sense of what happened and how it could have been avoided. Samantha’s bank job has become a significant source of anxiety for her. She often feels watched by customers or coworkers, which triggers her memories and makes her feel unsafe. This constant fear leads her to avoid making eye contact with others at work, further isolating herself and affecting her interactions. The cycle that Samantha experiences is self-reinforcing: her triggers activate her memory, which then intensifies her threat perception, leading to more avoidance behaviors like overanalysing the event or spending impulsively. These maladaptive strategies provide only temporary relief but ultimately exacerbate her symptoms by keeping her trapped in a loop of heightened anxiety and distress. What finally brought Samantha to seek help was her growing realization that she couldn’t function normally at work anymore without feeling constantly threatened. Her relationship with her husband has also suffered, as he struggles to understand her behavior and the reasons behind it. She is most afraid that these memories will never leave her and that she will continue to feel unsafe in everyday situations. Samantha hopes for a way to break this cycle of fear and distress, finding some peace and normalcy in her life once again. Despite the challenges ahead, she is determined to regain control over her thoughts and behaviors and reclaim a sense of safety and stability.
